GROWING IN MORALITY - STUDY NOTES

OPENING QUOTE
- Mark Twain: "When I was a boy of fourteen, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be twenty-one, I was astonished at how much he had learned in seven years."
- The point: as we grow up, our view of others and of what is wise changes.

MATURITY
- We grow physically from childhood to adulthood and become physically mature.
- We also expect to become more mature emotionally and morally as we grow. Everyday sayings show this: "The wisdom of old age", "Growing old and wise", "Leave your childish ways behind you!"
- But moral maturity does NOT automatically appear at any particular age.
- People do foolish, hurtful deeds and act immaturely at all ages.
- Young people can often show wisdom and maturity that older people do not have.
- We speak of the idealism of youth and, sadly, sometimes of the cynicism of old age.
- Being mature does not have to mean being boring.
- Movie example: Jim Sheridan's film In America (2003). The daughters, especially the elder daughter Christine, bring wisdom and clarity to their father, who has not been able to mourn properly the death of his child.
- Moral maturity is not an exact science like biology or physics. There are no definite laws of moral growth.
- But there are patterns of behaviour we can analyse, and a pattern of healthy growth towards maturity.
- Discussion examples of moral maturity: a parent who cares for a handicapped child; a young person who cares for elderly grandparents at home; a person who listens and gives good advice.

THE POEM "THE GOOD" BY BRENDAN KENNELLY
- The good are vulnerable, like "any bird in flight".
- They do not think of safety and are blind to possible extinction.
- When they are most vulnerable they are most themselves.
- The good incline to praise; they have the knack of seeing that the best is not destroyed, although forever threatened.
- They always keep "a kind of youth", the vulnerable grace of a bird in flight.
- They are "Accomplished master and potential victim", accepting what earth or heaven intends.
- The poet ends: "I think that I know one or two / Among my friends." (good people are found among ordinary people we know).

DEFINING MORAL MATURITY
- The idea becomes clearer when we think of real people who show us what it means to be moral.
- History gives examples of people who showed moral virtue and made sacrifices for a truth.
- Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King: seen as morally mature because both showed great moral courage in choosing a path of non-violence to achieve justice for their peoples.
- In our own lives we may know mature people who do not care what others think of them and are happy with the way they are, or who have life experience and give good advice.

CHARACTERISTICS OF A MORALLY MATURE PERSON
- Has a sense of right and wrong.
- Thoughtful and considerate of how actions will affect others.
- Able to reflect and work things out for themselves.
- Open to listening to others: not arrogant.
- Independent and strong: able to stand by their decisions even if they are unpopular.
- Has moral courage.
- Has the ability to listen to criticism.

CHARACTERISTICS OF A MORALLY IMMATURE PERSON
- No real sense of right and wrong.
- Childish.
- Selfish.
- Looking after their own interests.
- Just looking for their own pleasure.
- Following the crowd.
- Not thinking things through.
- Not reflective.
- Impulsive.
- Trying to please others.
- Low self-esteem.

THEORIES OF DEVELOPMENT
- Much study has been done on how we develop: how we come to know the world, how we develop intellectually and how we develop morally. Theorists do not all agree on the main influences.
- Sigmund Freud (1856-1939): the most controversial and original theorist. He highlighted the influence of parents during infancy on a person's development.
- Behaviourists: a group of theorists who believed the child was a "clean slate", totally shaped by the environment.
- A behavioural (developmental) theory suggests that there are definite stages of moral development.

JEAN PIAGET (1896-1980)
- Swiss psychologist.
- Wrote about children's "cognitive development" - how their understanding develops.
- In the 1960s, using surveys and analysis, he studied the influence of genetics and environment on human behaviour.
- He found that the way people think shapes their morality.
- Age 5 to 8: children are very self-centred; morality is seen as rules imposed by others.
- Age 10 onwards: the person's thinking takes in the intentions of others. The child begins to have moral values that lead to a good life and begins to follow rules by choice.
- Piaget influenced later moral theorists such as Lawrence Kohlberg.

LAWRENCE KOHLBERG (born 1927)
- Applied Piaget's developmental approach to moral development.
- Also strongly influenced by Immanuel Kant.
- Method: surveys with children - he gave them moral dilemmas and asked them to evaluate the moral conflict.
- His theory: stages of moral development build on each other; each stage is more complex than the one before in understanding and knowledge.
- Three levels, each split into two stages (six stages in total).
- Each level has a basic moral value at work. Each stage decides how a person makes a moral decision.

LEVEL I: PRE-CONVENTIONAL MORALITY (AGE 4-10) - NEEDS AND WANTS
- Moral value lies in a person's own needs and wants.
- Stage 1: Obedience-Punishment Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by the need to avoid punishment. Example: Little Hugh will not hit his sister because he does not want to get shouted at.
- Stage 2: Instrumental-Relativist Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by the need to satisfy one's own desires. Example: if toddler Hugh tidies his room he will get sweets.

LEVEL II: CONVENTIONAL MORALITY (AGE 10-13) - PLEASING OTHERS
- Moral value lies in keeping the conventional order and pleasing others.
- Stage 3: "Good Boy/Nice Girl" Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by the need to avoid disapproval from others. Example: Good boy Hugh will not disturb Maths class because the teacher will get a bad impression of him.
- Stage 4: Law and Order Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by the need not to be criticised by an authority figure. Example: Careful Hugh will not smoke in school because it is against the rules.

LEVEL III: POST-CONVENTIONAL MORALITY (ADOLESCENCE/ADULTHOOD) - PRINCIPLES
- Moral values lie in principles.
- Stage 5: Legalistic Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by respect for social order, human rights and living under legally determined laws. Example: Respectful Hugh drives within the speed limit because that is the law of the land.
- Stage 6: Universal, Ethical Orientation. Moral judgement is driven by one's own conscience. Example: Conscientious Hugh keeps the speed limit because he wants to respect his life and that of others.

ADULTS AND THE STAGES
- Adults can still operate out of these stages.
- Stage 1: any behaviour driven by the prospect of pleasure or pain. Example: a soldier carrying out an atrocity in war to avoid being killed.
- Stage 2: summed up as "You scratch my back, I'll scratch yours" - I will get what I need for myself. Quite a few adults still work at this level.
- Stage 3: summed up as conformity - "Everyone is doing it, so it must be okay." The big sin would be to do something different.
- Stage 4: respect for law and order and authority in general. Justice is seen as punishment for breaking the law; a strong sense of responsibility to the social order.
- Stage 5: general moral principles are applied to situations. The person acts out of obligation to others and a sense of public good. Society should only limit an individual's freedom when it infringes on someone else's freedom.
- Stage 6: the person acts out of the principle of the Golden Rule: people are not means to ends; they have rights and responsibilities.

SUMMARY OF KOHLBERG
- Pre-conventional level: morality based on the consequences of the behaviour.
- Conventional level: moral judgements based on the expectations of society.
- Post-conventional level: values and principles guide moral judgements.
- You must go through the stages in order; you cannot reach a higher stage without passing through the stage just before it.
- For Kohlberg, the morally mature person would be one at the post-conventional level, guided by principles and conscience.

CRITIQUE OF KOHLBERG
- Carol Gilligan: the higher stages are biased toward male characteristics. Women move toward maturity in different ways to men, having a different sense of connectedness with others.
- Other theorists: Kohlberg focuses too much on reasoning and judgement. Moral development has more to do with developing moral character, values and virtues.
- Assignment idea: Erik Erikson's theory is perhaps the best example of moral development seen to evolve through practising human virtues. He has eight stages of development.

SHAPING MORAL PRINCIPLES - SOURCES OF MORALITY
- Our personal value system is shaped by many factors close to us. We cannot make decisions alone without information and guidance.
- Information and opinion come to us through "filters" that colour and shape what we learn and help form our own opinions.
- Six sources of moral influence: family, peers, culture, media, religion, life experience.
- Family: probably the greatest factor in moral development. If our family values honesty, that value will probably matter to us too. We might also react against a family value (e.g. parents value close contact with relations but we decide it is unimportant). Family influence is complex and often subtle, with hidden and expressed messages.
- Peers: at a certain stage, people our own age (friends) shape our views. Through discussion and even conflict with peers we come to understand ourselves, our world and what is important.
- Culture: story of a fish in the sea looking for the ocean - nobody knows where it is, though it is all around them. Modern culture is like the ocean: we are so immersed in it we fail to see it and can drift along in it. Culture has been described as a lens, a transmitter, a set of blinkers, a womb and a menu.
- Media: radio, television, movies, newspapers, music, magazines, the Internet all communicate culture and shape information in a particular way. Current affairs and documentaries highlight moral issues and open up other worlds. But the media can also be used for propaganda - to promote someone or something, or to show them in a bad light.
- Religion: has much to teach on ethics, from scriptures to lived faith. Lived faith gives direction, motivation and purpose to live morally. The lives of people of faith can deeply affect others. In the modern Western world, people are encouraged to question traditional authorities (government, church leaders).
- Life experience: all that happens to us shapes us. Living a year in a poor third world country might shape views on justice; living in a war-torn country might shape views on war and peace; experiencing injustice from authority might shape how we view the law.
- Group discussion quote from German theologian Johann Baptist Metz: "The Church has lost its appeal, not because it is too demanding on people, but rather because it is not demanding enough."
- Church scandals have contributed to the loss of respect for the teaching authority of the churches.
- Research resources: David Tuohy and Penny Cairns, Youth 2K (Marino Institute of Education); Tom Beaudoin, Virtual Faith: The Irreverent Spiritual Quest of Generation X.

CASE STUDY: SEXUALITY AND YOUNG PEOPLE
- Family view: sex never spoken about at home, but great upset if a teenager became a parent. Effect: awkwardness, guilt about sex.
- Peers' view: sex is part of relationships and fun, but can leave people feeling used. Effect: you have to be careful.
- Cultural view: sex is for recreation; a perception that everyone is doing it. Effect: it's okay after all.
- Media view: sex is always exciting, passionate and glamorous. Effect: I can't be left out.
- Church view: sexual intercourse is only for those in a totally committed relationship. Effect: I have to wait for the perfect partner - patience or frustration.
- Life experience: she would not have sex with her boyfriend, so he dumped her; "boys are just in it for one thing". Effect: hurt.
- Lesson: it is important to be aware of the influences on us and the weight we give each source of morality before making a moral decision.

FREEDOM
- Freedom can mean different things to different people.
- We first think of freedom FROM something that holds us back. Examples: finishing the Leaving Cert ("free from school"); Nelson Mandela set free from prison on Robben Island after twenty-six years; "I'm free to do what I want, any old time!"
- Human freedom: freedom from oppression; being in control of our lives.
- Moral freedom: goes further. Freedom is a gift. We are free to choose between good and evil and to choose what type of person we become. Without this there would be no moral problems.
- Genesis story: the first humans were free to choose whether or not to eat the fruit of the tree.
- Limits to human freedom: with a moral vision, people do not have total freedom to do whatever they like (not free to hurt everyone you meet). Society limits freedom for the common good, even denying freedom to those who break a law.
- Free will (religious context): freedom is at the heart of the Christian understanding of the person. God made us free to respond to or reject the God of love. God totally respects human dignity and freedom. Disciples are called to follow Christ - to respond.

CHRISTIAN FREEDOM - ST PAUL
- If one is of Christ, believes in Christ and lives in Christ, one is totally free. There is no need for the Law.
- Life in the Spirit means being guided by the Spirit. All that counts is faith working through love.
- The follower of Christ is free from the slavery of sin - the greatest possible freedom.
- Even all creation will be set free from its bondage to decay, because Christ has set us free from death through his resurrection.
- Galatians 5:1, 13: "For freedom Christ has set us free. Stand firm, therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery... For you were called to freedom... only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for self-indulgence, but through love become slaves to one another." (See also Romans 8:18-24.)

VIRTUE AND VIRTUE ETHICS
- If morality is about personal growth and becoming a good person, we must understand virtue.
- Philippians 4:8: "Whatever is true, whatever is honourable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is pleasing, whatever is commendable... think about these things."
- Virtue: the word comes from the Greek word for excellence.
- Foundations of virtue ethics: the Greek philosopher Aristotle and the theologian Thomas Aquinas.
- Aristotle: "A virtue is a kind of second nature that disposes us to do the right thing rightly but also to gain pleasure from what we do."
- St Augustine: virtue is a quality of inner goodness through which one lives well and avoids acting badly.
- Dispositions: the inclinations within us that guide our actions. A virtue guides our dispositions to do the good.
- Catechism of the Catholic Church (para. 1803): a virtue is "a habitual and firm disposition to do the good".
- Richard Gula: this view "sees the moral life reflected more in the quality of our character and in our relationships than in the isolated actions that we do".
- Virtue ethics looks at a person's whole character, not just single actions. Instead of "What am I doing?" we ask "What sort of person am I becoming because of my actions?"
- Also called "character ethics": the more we nourish and live out virtues, the more virtuous we become.

VIRTUES AND VIRTUE
- A person of virtue (virtuous person): has the strength of character to carry out a vision for life.
- St Thomas More: example from history of a virtuous person who lived and died by his principles. One virtue that guided him was courage.
- We can also speak of the specific virtues a person has that guide their actions.
- Br Roger of Taize is pictured in the chapter as a person of virtue.
- The revision questions name wisdom, courage, temperance and justice as virtues to look for in people today.

CRITIQUE OF VIRTUE ETHICS
- Some believe it is impossible to agree on which virtues are central and to classify them as Aquinas did.
- So many moral philosophers have placed virtues in a secondary position to rules and laws.

TEMPERANCE
- Gives a person a sense of balance in life; one is not acting out of a compulsion that controls one's life.
- Examples of living out of compulsion: addiction to drugs, especially alcohol; addiction to gambling; shopping addiction.
- Temperance gives discipline over one's own life so one can reach true goals. Any goal involves decisions and sacrifice.
- Examples: the athlete who trains and sacrifices to succeed; the student studying for an exam.

HOPE
- Hope is a theological virtue. Many feel it is the virtue most needed in today's culture.
- In hope we desire happiness, place our trust in God and know the grace of the help of the Holy Spirit.
- Hope is different from optimism. An optimist thinks all will turn out okay and has a cheerful outlook, not wanting to see the negative. A person of Christian hope puts all their trust in God and knows that, even with great darkness of evil in the world, the light is and will be victorious.
- Jurgen Moltmann (Theology of Hope): hopelessness is totally destructive. The hopeless person rejects the promises of God. It is not so much the evil a person does, but their failure to do good that destroys their relationship with God. The sin of despair comes from losing one's sense of hope.
- Despair is deepest when personal hopes are cruelly shattered: broken relationships (wondering if you can trust again); being let down by trusted people such as church leaders; corruption preventing social justice.
- Christian hope is the opposite of despair: total confidence in the power of goodness; courage to keep working for justice, trusting people, believing in the good.
- Kierkegaard (philosopher): hope becomes a passion for what is possible; it gives people deep spiritual energy to follow their goal in life.

CHAPTER SUMMARY
- Moral maturity and immaturity are linked with how we develop from children to adults.
- Theorists such as Kohlberg suggest stages of moral development.
- Many factors influence our growth and decision-making.
- Moral freedom means we are free to choose our path.
- Christian freedom flows from following Christ totally.
- Virtue ethics sees moral growth as building moral character by developing virtues.

KEY TERMS
- Moral maturity: having a sense of right and wrong, reflecting, considering others and having the courage to stand by decisions - not tied to age.
- Stages of moral development: the levels and stages (e.g. Kohlberg's six) through which people grow in moral reasoning.
- Moral character: the kind of person we are, shown in our virtues, values and relationships.
- Sources of morality: the influences that shape our moral views - family, peers, culture, media, religion, life experience.
- Human freedom: freedom from oppression; being in control of our lives.
- Moral freedom: the gift of being free to choose between good and evil and what type of person to become.
- Virtue: a habitual and firm disposition to do the good (from the Greek for excellence).
- Virtue ethics: an approach to morality that focuses on building good character through virtues rather than on isolated actions (also called character ethics).

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words what Piaget discovered about how children's morality changes from age five to age ten.
rows.model_answer: Piaget found that the way people think shapes their morality. Children aged five to eight are very self-centred and see morality as rules imposed by others. From about age ten, they begin to take in the intentions of others, develop moral values and follow rules by choice.

rows.prompt: Name Kohlberg's three levels of moral development and the basic moral value of each.

rows.prompt: Outline Lawrence Kohlberg's theory of moral development, referring to its levels and stages. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Lawrence Kohlberg applied Jean Piaget's developmental approach to moral development and was also influenced by Immanuel Kant. He gave children moral dilemmas and asked them to evaluate them. He believed the stages build on each other, each more complex than the last, and that a person must pass through them in order. There are three levels, each with two stages. Level I, Pre-conventional Morality (age 4-10), is based on needs and wants. In Stage 1 (Obedience-Punishment) a person acts to avoid punishment, e.g. Hugh won't hit his sister so he won't be shouted at. In Stage 2 (Instrumental-Relativist) a person acts to satisfy their own desires: 'you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours'. Level II, Conventional Morality (age 10-13), is about pleasing others. Stage 3 (Good Boy/Nice Girl) avoids disapproval and is about conformity; Stage 4 (Law and Order) respects rules and authority. Level III, Post-conventional Morality (adolescence/adulthood), is based on principles. Stage 5 (Legalistic) respects social order, human rights and laws; Stage 6 (Universal Ethical) follows one's own conscience and the Golden Rule. In summary, morality moves from consequences, to society's expectations, to principles.

rows.prompt: Describe how any three sources of morality can shape a young person's moral views. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Our personal values are shaped by many influences, which act like filters colouring what we learn. Family is probably the greatest factor. If a family values honesty, that value is likely to matter to the young person, though they may also react against a family value. Family messages are often subtle, some hidden and some expressed; for example, if sex is never spoken about at home, a teenager may feel awkward or guilty about it. Peers become very important at a certain stage. Through discussion and even conflict with friends, young people come to understand themselves and what matters; peers might say sex is fun but can leave people feeling used. The media - radio, TV, films, newspapers, music, magazines and the Internet - communicate culture and shape information in particular ways. Documentaries can open up moral issues in other worlds, but the media can also be used for propaganda, and it can present sex as always exciting and glamorous, making a young person feel 'I can't be left out'. All these sources influence the type of person we become, so it is important to be aware of them and of the weight we give each one.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by moral freedom and outline the Christian understanding of freedom. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: We often think of freedom as freedom from something that holds us back, like finishing the Leaving Cert or Nelson Mandela being released from Robben Island after twenty-six years. This is human freedom: freedom from oppression, being in control of our lives. Moral freedom goes further. It is a gift: we are free to choose between good and evil and to choose what type of person we become. Without it there would be no moral problems. In Genesis, the first humans were free to choose whether to eat the fruit of the tree. Freedom has limits: we are not free to hurt others, and society limits freedom for the common good. In a religious context we speak of free will. Freedom is at the heart of the Christian understanding of the person: God made us free to respond to or reject the God of love and fully respects our dignity. For St Paul, if one lives in Christ, one is totally free, with no need for the Law; life in the Spirit means being guided by the Spirit, and all that counts is faith working through love. The Christian is free from the slavery of sin. Galatians 5 warns not to use freedom for self-indulgence but through love to serve one another.

rows.prompt: What is virtue ethics? Explain with reference to the virtues of temperance and hope. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Virtue ethics is an approach to morality that sees the moral life as personal growth - becoming a good person. The word virtue comes from the Greek for excellence, and the approach is founded on Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas. Aristotle said a virtue is a second nature that disposes us to do the right thing rightly and to take pleasure in it. The Catechism (para. 1803) defines virtue as a habitual and firm disposition to do the good. Richard Gula says the moral life is reflected more in our character and relationships than in isolated actions. So instead of asking 'What am I doing?' we ask 'What sort of person am I becoming?' This is also called character ethics. Temperance gives balance in life so a person is not controlled by compulsions such as addiction to alcohol, gambling or shopping. It gives discipline to reach true goals, like an athlete training or a student studying. Hope is a theological virtue, perhaps the one most needed today. It means trusting in God and the help of the Holy Spirit. It differs from optimism: Christian hope trusts that light will win even amid evil. Moltmann warns that despair destroys our relationship with God, while for Kierkegaard hope is a passion for what is possible.

Temperance (up to 6): balance, not compulsion, addictions, discipline, sacrifice for goals. Hope (up to 6): theological virtue, trust in God, Holy Spirit, differs from optimism, despair (Moltmann), Kierkegaard's passion for the possible.

rows.prompt: Describe the characteristics of a morally mature person. Refer to one example of a morally mature person in your answer. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: Moral maturity does not come automatically with age; young people can be wiser than adults. A morally mature person has a sense of right and wrong and thinks about how their actions will affect others. They can reflect and work things out for themselves and are open to listening to others rather than being arrogant. They are independent and strong, able to stand by their decisions even if unpopular, and they have moral courage and can listen to criticism. Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King are examples: both showed great moral courage in choosing a path of non-violence to achieve justice for their peoples, even at great personal cost.
